title: Web: tool catalog and approvals
summary: The tool catalog and approvals screens are careful where it matters most. Every read goes through the generated runtime parsers. A decision binds the argument hash shown on screen, and the list is re-read from the API instead of being updated optimistically. Request text is rendered as React text nodes only. The tool guide is a native modal that closes on the backdrop and Escape and returns focus. Playwright covers decisions, replay, tabs, J/K, the two-press shortcut, both request views, the modal's close paths and axe in both themes. The cost sits in two oversized client modules. approvals-panel.tsx has 773 lines, including a 308-line panel with nine useState hooks and a key handler with complexity 27. tool-catalog.tsx has 853 lines and eight components, plus pure text helpers that the Expert editor imports. Reading them in full surfaced defects where their responsibilities meet. A held ⌘↵ or Ctrl+↵ satisfies AP-04's second press, and the arm is not tied to a request. Decisions have no in-flight state, and the button and keyboard paths apply different truncation rules. The list fetch exists twice, because the project's react-hooks/set-state-in-effect rule forbids the obvious reuse, and the unguarded copy can put waiting requests under Decided. Each screen turns every load failure into one message with no retry, and that message is sometimes wrong. The recommended split fixes these without moving any decision out of the API: pure text, field and shortcut rules move to lib with node:test, one reloadable useLoaded hook serves both screens, decisions and shortcuts get their own hooks, and each detail surface gets its own file.

scores.why: Strict TypeScript flags and the project ESLint pass and colors are semantic, but DH-06's rules on duplicate submits, deliberate states and assertions are each missed, and the tool dialog departs from DS-03's dialog surface.

Dependencies run correctly from the generated client into the components, but pure text and a generic data hook live inside client component files, and the Expert editor imports from the catalog panel.
These are two of the five largest web files (773 and 853 lines), with functions of 308, 249, 245 and 174 lines and a key handler with complexity 27.
The small pure formatters at the top of approvals-panel are well separated, but onKey, ToolCatalogPanel and ToolDetail each mix state, URL handling and rendering.
The thin server pages and the flat, feature-prefixed components folder match the rest of apps/web, but four and eight components per file hide the area's shape.

The server stays authoritative, with no optimistic updates and a native modal, but fetching is hand-rolled twice, nine useStates carry an implicit state machine, and the two-press guard accepts key repeat.
Most comments explain why and trace to AP, TL, TG and Decision IDs; a few invariants are unstated, and two comments no longer match the code.
Generated types and runtime parsers are used at every read, but the label tables ignore the contract's unions and one error body is cast.
Each screen collapses every failure into one state, with copy that can be wrong ('sign in', 'not in the catalog'), no retry and the cause discarded.
Playwright covers the main flows and accessibility thoroughly, but the pure logic has no unit tests, and nothing covers held keys, races or failure states.
Readable, accessible and well traced, but the two oversized modules concentrate this area's defects; the split plus shared hooks would make it a model.

strengths.title: Runtime contract parsing on every read
strengths.evidence: approvals-panel.tsx:143 and 168 use parseApprovalList. tool-catalog.tsx:192, 582-585 and 780-783 parse through useLoaded with parseToolCatalog, parseToolVersions and parseToolGrants. These are backed by parseWith in packages/api-client/src/runtime.ts:142-149, which rejects unknown enum values and missing fields.

strengths.title: A typed, abortable load hook worth promoting
strengths.evidence: tool-catalog.tsx:156-181 useLoaded returns a discriminated union (loading, unavailable, ready). It aborts on cleanup, ignores stale replies and turns parse errors into a visible state. It is the best fetch shape in the area, and 24 hand-rolled 'let active = true' effects elsewhere in apps/web/components could share it.

strengths.title: Server-authoritative decisions with no optimistic state
strengths.evidence: approvals-panel.tsx:195-206 posts through csrfFetch with an Idempotency-Key and binds the decision to approval.argument_hash. Lines 24-33 turn the API's refusal codes into plain words, and line 223 re-reads the list after the reply instead of editing it locally, as DH-06 asks ('browser state is a view of durable state').

strengths.title: Untrusted request content rendered safely and faithfully
strengths.evidence: approvals-panel.tsx:700-742 Markdown and inline build only React text nodes, and neither file uses dangerouslySetInnerHTML. At 686-698, parsedFields withholds the Fields view when JSON would reorder integer-like keys, which keeps AP-03's 'never reorders' promise.

strengths.title: Accessibility engineered in
strengths.evidence: tool-catalog.tsx:439-481 opens a native modal dialog with showModal, a form method='dialog' Close button and backdrop detection, and 422-429 returns focus. approvals-panel.tsx:391-395 uses a roving-tabindex list with aria-current, 362-368 a polite live announcement for the two-press shortcut, and 744-773 sr-only colons in dt/dd pairs. Axe checks assert this in tools.spec.ts:246-263 (both themes) and approvals.spec.ts:399-402.

strengths.title: Schema rendering driven by server-flattened fields
strengths.evidence: tool-catalog.tsx:483-579 renders the API's FieldDescriptor rows (path, type, required, constraints, public) as a captioned table with column and row scopes inside a focusable, named scroll region, instead of walking JSON Schema in the browser. Lines 739-751 keep the raw schema behind a disclosure, and 831-853 copies exactly the shown version's input schema (TL-03).

strengths.title: Exhaustive table typing where it is used
strengths.evidence: tool-catalog.tsx:117-121 declares APPROVAL_TEXT as Record<ToolDescriptor['approval'], string>, so tsc fails if the contract adds an approval mode. This is the pattern to spread to the other label tables.

strengths.title: Comments that explain why and trace to requirements
strengths.evidence: approvals-panel.tsx:115-116 (AP-01 to AP-04), 232 (arrows only inside the list), 686 (integer-like keys) and 700 (text nodes only). tool-catalog.tsx:43 (state in words), 116 (Decision 0026 C9), 437-438 (G2/G3 native dialog), 458 (backdrop click) and 501 (axe scrollable-region rule).

findings.title: approvals-panel.tsx packs data loading, decisions, a shortcut state machine and two large views into one module

locations.note: ApprovalsPanel: 308 lines, complexity 11; fetches, decides, handles keys and renders tabs and list
nine useState hooks carrying one implicit state machine
keyboard machine and disarm timer inside the panel
ApprovalDetail: 245 lines, complexity 13: facts, exact request, diffs, alert, decision bar
five pure formatters that node:test cannot import from a 'use client' TSX module
Fields parser and a self-contained markdown renderer
Fact component

findings.evidence: Reading confirms the ESLint leads. ApprovalsPanel declares nine useState hooks (123-134), fetches the list (136-187), sends decisions (192-226), runs the two-press shortcut machine (228-298) and renders the tabs, messages and list (317-433). ApprovalDetail adds 245 more lines. The file also holds five formatters, parsedFields, Markdown and inline, and Fact: 4 components and 735 counted lines (max-lines rule).
findings.impact: Every change to the approval gate edits one 300-line closure. The defects found in this area sit exactly where these responsibilities meet: a held key confirms a decision, a reload can land under the wrong tab, and the button and keyboard paths apply different guards. None of the pure logic can reach the node:test suite.
findings.recommendation: Split by responsibility without changing behavior, keeping every data-* hook and visible string so approvals.spec.ts passes unchanged. First, move the formatters, parsedFields and the shortcut rule to lib, with node:test cases. Then extract a reloadable useLoaded, useApprovalDecision and useApprovalShortcuts. Finally, move ApprovalDetail and its parts, and the markdown renderer, to their own files. ApprovalsPanel ends up holding tab and selection state plus composition.

findings.title: The two-press shortcut accepts a held key, Alt chords, and an arm that is not tied to a request

locations.note: onKey, complexity 27: navigation, focus moves and decision arming in one function; line 231 routes any meta, ctrl or alt chord to decisions
the second-press check never reads event.repeat
arm is { decision, until } with no approval id
list reload changes the selection without clearing the arm (again at 172)
button path decides without clearing the arm
documents ⌘ or Ctrl, not Alt
peer handler requires meta or ctrl and excludes alt
presses each chord discretely; no held key or Alt case

findings.impact: AP-04 requires a second press within 2 s. Holding ⌘↵ or Ctrl+↵ past the OS key-repeat delay fires a repeated keydown that counts as the second press, so one long press decides. The stale-arm path decides a request other than the one announced. The server still binds the decision to the hash shown, but the screen's confirmation step is bypassed.
findings.recommendation: Make the rule a pure function in lib/approval-shortcut.ts. Inputs: current arm, decision, approval id, now, repeat and truncated. Outputs: next arm, decision to send or none, and announcement. Cover repeat, Alt, approval change, expiry and truncation with node:test. Call it from useApprovalShortcuts, which subscribes once through React 19's useEffectEvent; react 19.3.1 is installed, and a stdin probe of this shape passes the project ESLint. The hook ignores event.repeat, requires (metaKey || ctrlKey) && !altKey, stores the approval id in the arm and clears the arm when the selection or pending state changes. Keep J/K/arrow navigation as its own small function. Add a browser case: hold Meta, call keyboard.down('Enter') twice (Playwright sends the second with repeat set), and expect no decision.
findings.ruleCheck: PRD-Studio AP-04 (PRD-Studio.md:99), and ground rule 2 against weakening an approval: this change tightens the confirmation. typing() still gates every shortcut, and the server's hash binding is untouched.
findings.verifierNote: No use of event.repeat exists in apps/web; line 231 routes Alt chords to decisions and the arm carries no id; a fresh ESLint stdin probe of the useEffectEvent hook passes. The held-key path is reasoned from the code, not observed.

findings.title: Decisions have no in-flight state, and the button and keyboard paths follow different rules

locations.note: decide: no pending flag; new Idempotency-Key per call (201); lost reply reported as a failure (220)
Approve and Reject never disabled; Approve stays live on truncated requests
keyboard path refuses truncated approvals before sending
peer: busy state disables submit (142, 188)
peer: lost reply or 5xx is an unknown outcome, not a failure
server replays a same-decision repeat

findings.evidence: decide() sets no pending flag. Approve and Reject stay enabled across the CSRF fetch, the POST and the reload, and each click mints a new Idempotency-Key (201). The keyboard path refuses to approve a truncated request before sending (265-268). The Approve button sends it and waits for the server's approval_too_large refusal. A null reply (lost connection) shows 'That decision couldn't be saved.' (220), although the API may have committed.
findings.impact: DH-06 asks for duplicate submits to be disabled, with server idempotency as the correctness mechanism; only the server half exists here. Double clicks send duplicate POSTs and race two reloads. The truncation rule has two homes with different behavior. A lost reply asserts a failure that the reloaded list may contradict. No optimistic update is made, which is correct and should stay.
findings.recommendation: Extract useApprovalDecision(reload) returning { pending, message, decide }. Set pending before the request and clear it in finally; disable both buttons while pending, and have the shortcut hook ignore presses while pending. Give the truncation rule one home: either derive canApprove once from the server's arguments_truncated flag and use it for both the button and the shortcut, or drop the client check from both and rely on the refusal. For reply === null or status >= 500, say the outcome is not known yet and let the reloaded list show it, as continue-run.tsx does.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06 'Disable duplicate submits with server idempotency as the correctness mechanism' and 'avoid duplicated business rules'. The API's hash binding and refusal codes stay authoritative, and no state transition moves into Next.js.
findings.verifierNote: The buttons at 664-675 never disable, the keyboard refuses truncated approvals at 265-268 while the button sends, and the server replays a same-decision repeat at approvals.py:278-281.

findings.title: The approval list fetch exists twice, and the unguarded copy can show waiting requests under Decided

findings.impact: Switching to Decided while a decision is in flight lets load('waiting') finish after the Decided fetch and replace the list. That contradicts the invariant stated at line 337, and the waiting requests then render with Decided labels. The two copies have already drifted (duplicate setCounts, different error handling).
findings.recommendation: Keep one guarded fetch path and reload through it. A shared useLoaded(path, parse) keeps a reload counter in the effect's dependencies, aborts on cleanup and returns { state, reload }; decide() calls reload() instead of fetching. A stdin probe of this shape passes the project ESLint. Make the selection fallback (keep the current id if still listed, else the first) a pure function called from one place.
findings.ruleCheck: The project ESLint react-hooks/set-state-in-effect rule still holds, since setState stays inside the async callbacks. DH-06 'Browser state is a view of durable state'.
findings.verifierNote: A fresh ESLint stdin probe reproduces react-hooks/set-state-in-effect for an effect that calls load(), and a reload-counter hook passes; the duplicate setCounts is at 170-171 and operations-panel.tsx:165-200 has the same pair.

findings.title: Every load failure becomes one message with no retry, and some messages are wrong

locations.note: 'Sign in, then try again.' for any failure; tabs hidden; no retry
status and error discarded into a boolean
useLoaded keeps only { kind: 'unavailable' } for status, network and ContractError
'Check that the local service is running' also for 401 and 403
'That tool isn't in the catalog.' also for 401, 403 and 503
a tool with no versions renders nothing
BFF already returns 403 and 401 (and 503 at 120)
peer screen words 403 separately

findings.evidence: Neither file reads the reply status. The BFF distinguishes refusals (403), not_signed_in (401) and service_unavailable (503), and operations-panel.tsx and run-inspector.tsx word them separately. Here, Approvals says 'Sign in, then try again.' for every failure and replaces its tabs. The catalog blames the local service for auth failures. The detail page says a tool is not in the catalog when the session expired or the API is down. None of the four states offers a retry.
findings.impact: DH-06 requires loading, empty, denied, unavailable and retryable states to be represented deliberately. A stopped API tells a signed-in owner to sign in, an expired session says the tool doesn't exist, and contract drift looks like an outage with no trace. If the reload fails right after a successful decision, the sign-in message replaces the confirmation, and only a full page reload recovers.
findings.recommendation: Give the shared load hook a typed failure reason: signed_out for 401, denied for 403, not_found for 404, unavailable for 5xx or network errors, and invalid for a ContractError. Render one shared failure component with reason-specific copy and a Retry button bound to reload(). Keep the approvals tabs visible on failure. Log a ContractError's path to the console in development, since it carries no secret. Render an explicit empty state for a tool with no versions.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06 'Represent loading, empty, denied, unavailable and retryable states deliberately' and 'preserve causes in private logs and expose safe typed errors'. The user-facing copy reveals no server detail.
findings.verifierNote: Neither file reads reply.status; the BFF returns 401, 403 and 503 with distinct codes (bff.ts:53-57, 120); a failed reload after a decision leaves only the sign-in text, since the tabs are not rendered.

findings.evidence: Reading confirms the leads: the group callback runs 97 lines and the row callback 64, and there are eight components in 853 lines. The panel interleaves URL state, filtering (218-227), the toolbar and the grouped list. It filters shown by group three times instead of reusing inGroup. The TS-01 row wording is assembled inline (372-390). FieldTable receives the whole ToolDescriptor but needs only its fields and title, repeats <th scope='col' className='pr-3 pb-2 font-medium'> five times and builds constraint text inline as `${key} ${JSON.stringify(value)}`. Its table semantics are good and should stay: caption, column and row scopes, and a focusable, named scroll region (501-507).
findings.impact: Adding a filter, a row fact or a detail field means editing a 250-line function that mixes URL, filter and markup logic. The row wording and the constraint wording cannot be tested on their own, and changing a field column means editing several places.
findings.recommendation: Split following the repository's flat feature-prefix convention (as the run-*.tsx files do): move pure parts to lib first, then give each surface its own file. Group once with a Map and pass each group's tools down. Give FieldTable a { title, caption, fields } signature with a COLUMNS constant and a FieldRow, let ToolDetail split fields by direction once, and move constraintText to lib/tool-text.ts with tests. Behavior and data-* hooks, data-fields and data-field-path included, stay as they are, so tools.spec.ts covers the move.

The browser suites are strong: decisions and replay, tabs, J/K, two-press, typing guard, Fields/JSON with axe, modal close paths, focus return and Copy schema. findings.impact: The rules most likely to regress here are checked only by slow end-to-end runs: the two-press machine, AP-03's no-reorder rule, text-only markdown and the repair wording. The held-key and stale-reload defects in this area passed those runs.
findings.recommendation: Once the pure code has moved to lib, add node:test files for approval-shortcut (repeat, Alt, approval change, expiry, truncation), approval-text and relative-time boundaries, parsedFields (integer-like keys, arrays, truncation), markdown inline splitting and the tool-text repair branches. Register each file in the web_unit_tests step, or switch that step to a glob, which would also pick up schema-value.test.ts. Add browser cases for a held chord, a tab switch during a decision and a BFF 503.

findings.title: Label tables are typed Record<string, …> although the contract gives exact unions

GROUP_ICONS keyed by string; '?? Wrench' at 322 and 607

ToolDescriptor declares each of these fields as a union

findings.evidence: ToolDescriptor declares provider, operation_class, cost_class, availability and group as literal unions, and the generated runtime schema rejects any other value. Yet six tables in tool-catalog.tsx are keyed by string. Counted by grep, there are 12 lookups (11 here and 1 in expert-editor.tsx), and 11 of them carry a '?? tool.x' or '?? Wrench' fallback that cannot run after parsing.
findings.impact: When the Pydantic contract gains a provider, class, cost class or group, tsc stays green and the screen shows the raw snake_case id; nothing points at the table to update.
findings.recommendation: Type each table by its union, for example const PROVIDERS: Record<ToolDescriptor['provider'], string> and const AVAILABILITY_FILTERS: readonly ToolDescriptor['availability'][]. Then delete the fallbacks, so tsc fails at the table when the contract adds a value. Declare MESSAGES as const satisfies Record<string, string>. ApprovalView.status and operation_class are plain strings in the contract (generated.ts:7457, 7467). Narrowing them to Literals in the Pydantic DTO and regenerating would let OUTCOME become exhaustive too.
findings.ruleCheck: Contracts rule: Pydantic owns the contract, generated TypeScript consumes it, and unknown enums fail at runtime; this adds the compile-time half. No generated file is edited by hand.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 12 lookups, 11 with a fallback that parsing makes unreachable; downgraded from medium to low because nothing is wrong today and the fallbacks degrade gracefully to the raw id.

findings.evidence: There are four helpers, counted by grep for relative-time functions. Approvals reads 'in 5 min' where Home reads 'in 5 minutes'. In approvals, Math.round turns an expiry 20 s in the past into -0, which `minutes >= 0` reads as 'in 0 min'. now only advances when the list reloads, so 'Expires in 3 min' stays on screen as time passes.
findings.impact: The same kind of time reads differently on Home and in Approvals, and a request can show a future expiry after it has expired. The next fix will land in one copy only.

findings.evidence: The input uses defaultValue={params.get('q') ?? ''}, which is read only on mount. Following the sidebar's Tools link from /tools?q=calc keeps the panel mounted, because no template.tsx remounts it. The filter clears, but the box still shows 'calc'.
findings.impact: The visible query and the applied filter can disagree, breaking the promise that the URL holds the filter state.

findings.evidence: ToolDetail depends on the server's sort for 'newest', and nothing documents that order. AVAILABILITY_FILTERS omits not_qualified without a comment. useLoaded would loop on an inline parser, and nothing tells callers to pass a module-level function. The comments at approvals-panel.tsx:337 (no stale list) and tool-catalog.tsx:424 (first-link fallback) describe behavior the code does not have.
findings.impact: A server-side reorder, a caller passing an inline parser, or a well-meant cleanup of the filter list would break the screen silently. Comments that disagree with the code mislead the next change.
findings.recommendation: Pick the newest version by maximum version number, or document the order in the Pydantic field description so it reaches the generated contract. Add one-line why-comments for the filter list, the separate counts state and useLoaded's stable-parse requirement, or read parse through useEffectEvent. Use NOT_RECORDED at line 473, and fix the two comments together with the code changes they describe.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06 'Explain nonobvious invariants in code; avoid comments that restate syntax'. A change to the Pydantic description reaches TypeScript only by regeneration.
findings.verifierNote: versions.at(-1) relies on the sort at tool_catalog.py:261 and ToolVersions declares no order; line 473 repeats NOT_RECORDED's exact text.

notCovered: This was a static review. Ground rules ruled out running the app, a browser suite or tsc. Three claims are therefore reasoned from the code and standard browser and App Router behavior, not observed: a held ⌘↵ or Ctrl+↵ counting as the second press, the tab switch during an in-flight decision, and the stale search box after following the sidebar link. ESLint ran only on stdin probes, writing no files, to check the recommended hook shapes (a reload counter, and useEffectEvent) against the project config, and to confirm that react-hooks/set-state-in-effect rejects an effect that calls load(). Several files were read only in part: PRD-Development-Harness.md (DH-03 to DH-06), metrics.md, the PRD-Studio and PRD-Tool-Catalog sections for AP, TL, TS and TG, and decision 0026. The peer files cited for comparison or counts were read only around those lines: run-controls, continue-run, operations-panel, run-inspector, search-palette, new-run, home-activity, workflows-panel, experts-panel, run-list, expert-editor, about-services, sidebar-nav, lib/bff.ts, the two browser specs, scripts/verify.py and the Python approval and tool routes. Requirement coverage was not judged. TS-01 lists side effects per tool row, but `side_effects` is rendered nowhere in apps/web (grep), which acceptance owners may want to check. No comparison with an earlier review was made.
